status: authored teaching and mixed-skill checkpoint content; needs UI/audio and educator review; does not award SRS mastery
provenance: Original teaching text; standard pronunciation examples are independently attested in National Institute of Korean Language pronunciation rules and Q&A, with links per topic.

topics.title: Reading Hangul aloud: spelling versus pronunciation
topics.learningGoal: Recognize syllable blocks and several predictable sound changes before using audio-based lessons.

sections.heading: Syllable blocks and 받침
sections.explanation: Each written Korean syllable block contains a vowel and often an initial consonant plus a final consonant, called 받침. The final consonant's spoken sound is sometimes different from the letter's name.

examples.comment: At the end of a word, the final ㅊ is pronounced as a final [ㄷ]-type sound.

sections.heading: Liaison (연음)
sections.explanation: When a following particle begins with a silent initial ㅇ and a vowel, the final consonant often moves into the next spoken syllable. Keep the spelling unchanged.

examples.comment: The ㅊ sound moves to the next syllable before 이.
The ㄱ is heard at the beginning of the next spoken syllable.

sections.heading: Nasal assimilation (비음화)
sections.explanation: Some consonants become nasal sounds before ㄴ or ㅁ. This is why common words may sound different from their spellings.

examples.comment: The final ㄱ becomes [ㅇ] before ㄴ.

sections.heading: Aspiration with ㅎ
sections.explanation: In some combinations, ㅎ changes a nearby plain consonant into a stronger aspirated sound. These spelling-to-sound differences matter for listening.

examples.comment: ㅎ and ㄱ combine into the aspirated [ㅋ].

checks.prompt: How is 꽃이 usually pronounced in standard Korean?
checks.explanation: The final ㅊ moves before the vowel-initial particle 이: 꽃이 → [꼬치].
Final ㄱ becomes [ㅇ] before ㅁ: 국물 → [궁물].

choices: The particle 을 changes its spelling.
The final consonant links into the vowel-initial next syllable.
The word is in the past tense.
checks.explanation: Liaison changes pronunciation, not how the two parts are written.

topics.title: Respecting the listener versus respecting the subject
topics.learningGoal: Choose polite, casual and formal endings appropriately, and keep subject honorification separate from listener politeness.

sections.heading: To a listener you do not know
sections.explanation: Everyday polite -아요/-어요 is generally a safe starting point when addressing an adult stranger. It shows consideration toward the listener.

examples.comment: Polite speech can include both listener-facing -요 and a subject-honorific -시-.

sections.heading: To a close friend
sections.explanation: Close friends may agree to use the casual 해체 ending without 요. The relationship determines whether this sounds friendly or disrespectful.

examples.comment: The ending 해 is casual; using it with strangers without an appropriate relationship can sound rude.

sections.heading: Formal announcements
sections.explanation: Statements in -ㅂ니다/-습니다 are common in presentations, formal introductions, reports and public announcements. They are a register choice, not another tense.

examples.comment: 공부합니다 is a formal statement; 공부해요 is an everyday polite statement.

sections.heading: The person in the sentence
sections.explanation: -(으)시- and 께서 honor the subject, even when the listener is someone else. 께 marks a respected recipient instead.

examples.comment: 께서 and -시- both show respect to the teacher.

examples.english: I give the teacher a book.
examples.comment: 께 marks the respected recipient, not the subject.

checks.prompt: When first speaking to an adult stranger, which ending is usually safest?
checks.explanation: Everyday polite -요 forms are generally the safest default; context can call for more formality.

checks.prompt: In 선생님께서 오세요, who is being honored by -시-?
choices: The nearest noun regardless of role
checks.explanation: The subject-honorific -시- honors the person performing the action.

checks.prompt: Which particle marks a respected recipient rather than a subject?
checks.explanation: 께 marks the recipient. 께서 marks a respected subject.

topics.title: Use numbers in real sentences
topics.learningGoal: Combine early vocabulary for counting/time with grammar particles, without conflating mastery of the two.

sections.heading: Native hours, Sino minutes
sections.explanation: Korean typically says the hour using a native counting word but the minute using a Sino-Korean number. Keep the correct counter attached to each.

examples.comment: 세 is native, 십오 is Sino-Korean; 에 marks when the event occurs.

sections.heading: Counter choice follows the noun
sections.explanation: The lexical counter changes with the type of thing counted, while the sentence's grammar still determines the subject and object markers.

examples.comment: 명 counts people; 이 marks the subject of 있어요.
권 counts books; 을 marks the counted phrase as the object.

sections.heading: Some dates have irregular readings
sections.explanation: Month numbers use Sino readings, but the usual spoken readings of 6월 and 10월 are 유월 and 시월. The calendar words are vocabulary; they do not create extra grammar-point mastery.

examples.comment: Read 10월 as 시월, then 에 marks the time of the trip.

checks.explanation: Hours use native numbers (세 시); minutes use Sino numbers (십오 분).
권 is a counter for books and 네 is the native four form before counters.

checks.prompt: In 10월에 여행해요, what does 에 do?
choices: Mark the time of an action
checks.explanation: The month 10월 is vocabulary; 에 is the grammar particle locating when something happens.

topics.title: Who did it? Passive, causative and evidence
topics.learningGoal: Distinguish active/passive roles, causing an action and inferring rather than recalling firsthand evidence.

sections.heading: What happened versus who caused it
sections.explanation: Compare an active statement with the corresponding passive/result perspective. The choice determines who receives the main attention in the sentence.

examples.english: Minsu opened the door. The door opened.
examples.comment: The first sentence names the actor; the second describes the door's change.

sections.heading: Causing someone to act
sections.explanation: A causative describes one person making or letting another person do an action. Some verbs have their own causative partner; -게 하다 also works productively.

examples.english: The teacher had the students read books.
examples.comment: The teacher caused the students' reading action.

sections.heading: Remembering versus guessing
sections.explanation: -더라고요 recalls the speaker's firsthand observation. -나 보다 / -(으)ㄴ가 보다 expresses inference from a clue.

examples.english: I found the food at that restaurant tasty.
It seems to be raining outside.
examples.comment: The speaker infers rain from available clues.

checks.prompt: Which sentence focuses on the door as the thing affected?
checks.explanation: 문이 열렸어요 puts the door in subject position and describes its state change.

choices: Someone caused another person to read
checks.explanation: -게 하다 expresses causation or permission to perform an action.

checks.prompt: Which ending best recalls a firsthand discovery?
checks.explanation: -더라고요 usually looks back on what the speaker personally observed.
